book_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
question: How do DLF's two engines—luxury residential development and the DCCDL commercial annuity JV—actually work on the ground?

epigraph.quote: A developer builds once and sells once; a landlord builds once and collects rent for fifty years.
epigraph.author: Commercial Property Underwriting Principle

web_blocks.title: The Dual-Engine Architecture: Development vs. Annuity

web_blocks.html: DLF runs a two-track real estate model. It pairs high-margin home sales with steady commercial rent [6, 9]. The first track is the Development Business inside DLF Limited and its owned units [1, 9]. This unit turns old land into luxury condos, low-rise floors, and plotted townships, then sells them to buyers and investors [1, 9]. Over its history, DLF has finished 158+ projects totaling about 178 msf, or over 351 msf with group townships [1, 6, 9]. Today it has 27 msf under construction and 25 msf in its active launch pipeline [6]. Another 137 msf sits in balance land potential, including Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) and Transferable Development Rights (TDR) [1, 6, 9].

The second track is the Annuity Business. It spans about 50 msf of prime offices (44.6 msf at 96% leased) and retail malls (5 msf at 97% leased), with a Gross Asset Value (GAV) of ₹91,945 crore [6]. Roughly 44.3 msf of this active portfolio sits inside DLF Cyber City Developers Ltd (DCCDL), a 66.67% / 33.33% joint venture with Singapore's GIC [6, 9]. DLF holds another 3.2 msf directly on its own books [6]. A further 2.0 msf sits in Atrium Place, a JV where three towers have Occupancy Certificates and all four are leased [6, 7]. Estate upkeep, power units, and clubs like The Lodhi and DLF Golf & Country Club support both tracks [1, 6].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Example 1: An Ultra-HNI Family Buying at The Dahlias

web_blocks.html: To see how home sales work in practice, follow a Delhi business owner buying a 10,000 sq ft bare-shell home at The Dahlias on Golf Course Road (Sector 54, Gurugram) [10]. The buyer commits ₹70 crore to ₹100 crore (₹65,000–₹1,00,000+ per sq ft on super area, or over ₹1.5 lakh per sq ft on HRERA carpet area), plus 5% GST and stamp duty [10]. They sign a sale agreement under HRERA code RC/REP/HARERA/GGM/872/604/2024/99, which sets a December 2031 target for the Occupation Certificate (OC) [9, 10].

Over the next five years, the buyer pays build-linked tranches into a RERA bank account [9, 13]. By law, 70% of every rupee stays locked in that account for project land and build costs [9, 13]. DLF logs the ₹70–100 crore at once as pre-sales and books each payment as collections and contract liability [6, 13]. Yet it reports zero revenue and zero profit on its P&L until the tower gets its OC and keys change hands around 2031 [6, 13]. At The Dahlias alone, DLF booked ₹20,887 crore of sales by September 2026 [6]. About ₹14,410 crore of gross margin still sits off the P&L waiting for delivery [6].

web_blocks.title: Concrete Customer Example 2: A Global Capability Centre Leasing at DLF Cyber City

web_blocks.html: Now follow the rental engine. A Fortune 500 tech or finance firm opens a 2,000-seat Global Capability Centre (GCC) in Gurugram [6, 7]. It leases 200,000 sq ft in DLF Cyber City or Downtown Gurgaon through DCCDL [6, 7]. Unlike a homebuyer who pays once, the GCC signs a multi-year lease at an average portfolio rate of ₹110 per sq ft per month [6, 13]. That equals about ₹26.4 crore in yearly base rent from one tenant [6]. The lease also builds in regular rent hikes (often ~15% every three years) plus upkeep fees [6, 13].

DCCDL's 44.6 msf office book is 96% leased, and its 5 msf malls (DLF Promenade, Emporio, and Mall of India at ₹214 per sq ft per month) are 97% leased [6]. This rent stream acts much like a steady utility [6]. In Q2FY27 alone, DCCDL earned ₹1,482 crore in rent (₹1,222 crore office, ₹259 crore retail) and ₹752 crore in net profit [6]. It paid ₹420 crore in cash dividends up to DLF Limited [6]. In addition, 98% of DLF's buildings hold LEED Platinum status and 45 hold WiredScore Platinum, which helps keep blue-chip tenants [6].

web_blocks.title: Why the Two Engines Need Each Other
paragraphs: Luxury home sales bring high margins (45%+ gross margin on old land) and big upfront cash, but bookings swing wildly [6, 9]. They ranged from ₹11,000+ crore in a single launch quarter like Privana North down to ₹657 crore in a quiet quarter like Q1FY27 [6, 9].

DCCDL's ₹91,945 crore GAV rental book (₹99,640 crore with services and other assets) acts as a steady anchor [6, 9]. It covers firm overhead, funds dividends, and holds an AAA/Stable credit rating that shields DLF during housing slowdowns [6, 9].

book_paragraphs: To understand DLF, imagine two completely different businesses sharing the same roof. One is a sprint; the other is a marathon. Together, they explain why DLF looks very different from almost every other homebuilder in India.

The first engine is the Development Business. Here, DLF takes raw or legacy land it has owned for decades, designs luxury apartments or gated townships, and sells them off-plan to wealthy families and non-resident Indians. Across its history, DLF has delivered over 158 projects, and today it sits on 188 million square feet of total development potential—with 27 million square feet actively under construction and 25 million square feet in the upcoming launch pipeline.

In recent years, projects like The Arbour, the Privana cluster, and The Dahlias in Gurugram have sold out within days or months of launch. When a family buys an apartment, they pay in stages over four to six years while the towers are built.

Let us trace a real example. Suppose a business owner buys a ten-thousand-square-foot bare-shell residence at The Dahlias on Golf Course Road for ₹80 crore. Under India's real estate law, RERA, seventy percent of every instalment they pay goes straight into a locked project bank account that can only pay for that building's land and construction. Meanwhile, DLF's accountants cannot book a single rupee of that ₹80 crore as revenue on the income statement until the building receives its occupation certificate and the keys are handed over, roughly five years later. Across The Dahlias alone, DLF had booked ₹20,887 crore of sales by September 2026 with ₹14,410 crore of gross margin still sitting off the income statement awaiting completion.

The second engine is the Annuity Business, and it works like a toll road. Rather than selling buildings, DLF and its joint venture partner—Singapore's sovereign fund GIC—own roughly fifty million square feet of completed office parks and luxury shopping malls valued at nearly ₹92,000 crore. DLF owns two-thirds of this joint venture, called DCCDL, and GIC owns one-third.

Picture a multinational bank opening a two-thousand-person technology hub in DLF Cyber City. It signs a long-term lease for two lakh square feet, paying around ₹110 per square foot every month—roughly ₹26 crore a year in base rent from a single tenant—with automatic rent increases built into the contract. Next door, luxury brands in DLF's malls pay over ₹214 per square foot per month. With ninety-six percent of its offices and ninety-seven percent of its malls occupied, DCCDL collects predictable rent every single month, regardless of whether homebuyers are in a buying mood.

book_subsections.title: The Accounting Illusion You Must Spot
paragraphs: There is one quirk in DLF's financial statements that trips up almost every newcomer. Because GIC owns a third of DCCDL and holds minority governance rights, Indian accounting rules do not allow DLF to add DCCDL's ₹7,393 crore of annual revenue into DLF's own top line.

Instead, DLF only records its two-thirds share of DCCDL's net profit below the operating line, plus the cash dividends DCCDL sends upstream—such as ₹420 crore in a single quarter recently. When you read DLF's reported sales of ₹8,194 crore in fiscal 2026, remember you are looking at only half the empire. The other half is quietly compounding inside DCCDL, rated triple-A by credit agencies.

book_subsections.title: How Services and Sustainability Lock In Tenants
paragraphs: Supporting both engines are estate management, power distribution, and hospitality clubs like The Lodhi and the DLF Golf and Country Club. Nearly ninety-eight percent of DLF's commercial portfolio is LEED Platinum certified, and forty-five buildings hold top digital connectivity ratings. For global corporations choosing an Indian hub, that reliability justifies premium rents and keeps tenant churn low.

book_callouts.title: Two Engines, One Flywheel
book_callouts.text: Residential development turns legacy land into lump-sum cash; commercial leasing turns prime locations into recurring, inflation-protected dividends. Neither engine alone gives you the full picture of DLF.
